title: Choose & justify the target
goal: Pick one clearly identified study and the specific claim you will test, and write down why it is worth replicating now.
questions: Which study, and which exact claim or effect, will you test?
How valuable is it to know whether this claim is true?
How uncertain is the current evidence?
Is it feasible with your time, money, participants and skills?

fields.label: The specific claim / effect you will test
Existing reproductions / replications you found (e.g. in FReD)
Value: why knowing the truth of this claim matters (citations, theory, policy)
Uncertainty: why the current evidence is inconclusive (sample size, prior replications, design)
Your own potential biases toward a particular outcome
Decision & rationale (what would each possible outcome teach us?)

checklist.text: One target study and one specific claim are named
Searched for existing reproductions/replications of this claim
Value and uncertainty are both argued with evidence
Costs and feasibility are realistically assessed
Checked that the original design allows an informative replication
Selection rationale is written down transparently

title: Define aim & replication type
goal: State the purpose of your study, whether it is a reproduction or replication, how close it is to the original, and which replication goal your analysis will serve.
questions: What do you want to learn: whether the effect exists, how large it is, whether it generalises?
Close (direct) or conceptual (constructive) replication, and why?
How does this connect to theory?

fields.label: Replication goal (Anderson & Maxwell, 2016)
options: 3. How large is the effect (precise estimate)?
5. Is the replication clearly inconsistent with the original?
6. Is the replication clearly consistent with the original?

fields.label: Link to theory: what the result would mean for the theory

checklist.text: Purpose is stated before choosing design details
Replication type is named explicitly and justified
A replication goal is chosen (it determines the analysis in stage 9)
If conceptual/extension: a close replication is included first or justified
Checked that the design actually speaks to the original claim

title: Gather materials & contact authors
goal: Collect everything needed to rerun the original (materials, measures, procedure, data, code) and contact the original authors professionally.
questions: Which materials are public, which are missing?
Have you written to the original authors?
Have you read post-publication discussion of the study?

fields.label: What is missing, and how you will fill the gap
Author contact log (date, who, what was asked, response)

checklist.text: All original materials located or requested
Original authors contacted (use the email template)
Gaps in reported methods are documented, with how you filled them
Considered inviting authors to comment on your paradigm or an adversarial collaboration

title: Reproduce before you replicate
goal: Where data are available, rerun the original analysis on the original data to check the reported result before collecting new data.
questions: Are data and code available?
Do you get the same numbers?
Is the result robust to small, reasonable analytic changes?

fields.label: Which reported result you will reproduce

checklist.text: Attempted a reproduction (or explained why not possible)
Checked reported statistics for internal consistency
Documented software versions and seeds
Ran small, pre-specified robustness checks

resources.label: BITSS Guide for Advancing Computational Reproducibility (ACRE)

title: Check measurement & construct validity
goal: Make sure the measures in the original and in your replication produce valid scores. Without that, a success or failure is hard to interpret.
questions: What validity evidence exists for the original measures?
Will you translate or adapt anything?
How will you check the measure works in your sample?

fields.label: Validity evidence in the original (beyond Cronbach's alpha)
Validity checks you will run (factor structure, reliability, invariance, manipulation checks)

checklist.text: Validity evidence for each primary measure is summarised
Planned minimum validity checks in the new data
Translated/adapted measures have an equivalence plan
Decided what you will do if the measure fails

title: Plan design & sample size
goal: Choose a sample-size strategy that fits your replication goal. Don't simply reuse the original N.
questions: What is the original effect size and its confidence interval?
Which planning approach fits your goal?
What is the smallest effect size of interest?

fields.label: Original effect size, CI and N
Sample-size approach
options: Power for a conservative effect size
Equivalence test with a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI)

fields.label: Smallest effect size of interest & justification (if relevant)

checklist.text: Did not simply reuse the original sample size
Accounted for inflated original effect sizes
Approach matches the replication goal from stage 2
If aiming to show absence of an effect: sample is large enough for equivalence
Did not derive effect sizes from a small pilot

title: Document differences from the original
goal: List every difference between your study and the original, rate each one, and think ahead about which differences could change the result.
questions: What differs: population, setting, language, time, materials, procedure?
Which differences might plausibly matter, and why?
Can you test any of them?

fields.label: Differences that could plausibly change the result, and how you'll check them
Deliberate updates or improvements, and their justification
How your sample compares with the original

checklist.text: Every design component rated Exact / Close / Different
Plausibly influential differences identified in advance
Changes are 'as close as possible, as updated as necessary'
Measurement differences considered (not just procedure)

title: Preregister
goal: Fix hypotheses, design, exclusions, analysis and success criteria before seeing the data, or submit as a Registered Report.
questions: Where will you preregister?
Is a Registered Report possible?
What will you do if things go wrong (contingencies)?

checklist.text: Analysis plan and success criteria are preregistered
Primary effect(s) and how they are aggregated are specified
Exclusion rules set in advance
Region of equivalence set before data collection (if used)
Plan for reporting deviations

title: Analysis & success criteria
goal: Choose analyses that match your replication goal and define success and failure before you analyse the data.
questions: Which analysis matches your goal from stage 2?
What counts as success, failure, and inconclusive?
Will you run the original analysis, an updated one, or both?

fields.label: Primary analysis (matched to your replication goal)
How you will compare with the original (e.g. CI for the difference, equivalence)

checklist.text: Success criteria are defined before analysis
The analysis matches the chosen replication goal
Not relying only on 'significant vs. non-significant'
Not comparing p values or eyeballing CI overlap
Plan for careless responding and failed manipulation checks

resources.label: APA JARS — quantitative replication reporting table

title: Interpret, report & publish
goal: Interpret the results fairly, report everything openly, invite the original authors to comment, and find the right outlet.
questions: What does the evidence, taken as a whole, say?
Which explanations for divergence are plausible, and testable?
How will you frame the paper constructively?

fields.label: Outcome in balanced language (vs. your pre-set criteria)
Possible reasons for divergence (validity, differences, moderators)
Open materials, data and code; where results will be logged

checklist.text: Uses balanced, descriptive language about the outcome
Evaluates reasons for divergence carefully
Reports comprehensively and openly (materials, data, code)
Original authors invited to comment on results
Results logged in FReD
Does not treat one replication as conclusive
